scenes.headline: pandas: Cleaning & Transformation
scenes.subtitle: Turning messy data into analysis-ready tables
scenes.narration: Real-world data almost always arrives dirty, and cleaning it into analysis-ready tables is where data engineers genuinely spend most of their time.

scenes.headline: Common cleaning tasks
scenes.narration: Missing values propagate quietly through calculations, so deciding whether to fill or drop them is a first priority. Wrong dtypes, especially dates left as strings, block correct sorting and arithmetic until parsed. Duplicate rows silently inflate every aggregate, so they must be found and resolved. And inconsistent text, like mixed casing or stray whitespace, fragments what should be single categories.

scenes.headline: Handling missing data
scenes.code:
df['spend'] = df['spend'].fillna(0)
df = df.dropna(subset=['user_id'])
df['signup'] = pd.to_datetime(df['signup'], errors='coerce')
scenes.narration: Here fillna substitutes a sensible default for missing spend values so downstream sums stay valid. The dropna call removes rows lacking a user_id, since a record with no identity is usually unusable. And to_datetime with errors set to coerce parses the signup column, turning any unparseable value into a null rather than crashing the whole job.

scenes.headline: Transforming columns
scenes.code:
df['email'] = df['email'].str.strip().str.lower()
df['tier'] = df['spend'].apply(
    lambda x: 'high' if x > 100 else 'low')
df = df.rename(columns={'usr': 'user'})
scenes.narration: The vectorized str accessor lets you strip whitespace and lowercase every email in one pass, standardizing the column. The apply call derives a new tier column by mapping each spend value through a small function. And rename fixes a badly named header, keeping your schema clean and predictable for everything downstream.

scenes.headline: map vs apply vs applymap
scenes.narration: On a Series, map transforms each element and is ideal for simple value substitutions, while apply is more flexible and can run arbitrary logic per element. On a DataFrame, apply operates along an axis, running your function over whole rows or whole columns. Reach for map when the operation is a straightforward element-wise mapping, and apply when you need row-level or column-level logic.

scenes.headline: Pitfalls to avoid
scenes.narration: Chained indexing can assign to a temporary copy rather than the original, triggering the notorious SettingWithCopyWarning and silently losing your edit. Mutating a frame while iterating over it leads to unpredictable results. Ignoring the dtypes pandas inferred on read invites subtle numeric and date errors. And leaning on iterrows for row-by-row work is dramatically slower than a vectorized alternative.

scenes.headline: Cleaning pipeline
scenes.narration: A repeatable cleaning order keeps your work predictable and easy to review. Load the raw data first, correct the dtypes so later operations behave, then handle nulls, and finally normalize values like text and categories into consistent forms.

scenes.text: Assign with .loc, vectorize over .iterrows(), and coerce dtypes early to keep transforms correct and fast.
scenes.narration: Clean early, prefer vectorized operations over row loops, and assign through .loc so you never fall into the silent copy trap.
